WV12-P01.4.note: "It struck me only later that..." is the idiom for a realization coming to mind, so "occurred to" is the only sense that fits; nothing physical was hit, agreed, halted or erased.

support: On some evenings I still look up at a corner for the cream board and the black letters, the way you look for a face at the window of a house where someone used to live.
I have walked the old route once since, from Tanner Street down to the Gates.
WV12-P01.5.note: The author longs for signs that are gone, comparing the habit of looking for them to looking for a lost person; there is no praise of the craftsmanship as such (so not admiring), no fault-finding, no humor, and no worry since the boards are already destroyed.

support: I would give a great deal to hear the pitch of that hum again, low and steady, climbing a little on the hottest afternoons.
When I walk down Tamsin Lane in summer, I still stop at her gate for a moment, listening for a sound that went away to Dunmore long ago.
WV12-P02.5.note: The narrator yearns for the hives' sound that is now gone, which is wistfulness; the passage never judges the hives' quality (admiring/critical), shows no fear, and contains no humor.

WV12-P03.5.note: Answering a cheerful suggestion by recalling the torn-down kennel row where she first met Rook and saying she keeps picturing him there expresses longing for a vanished past; read literally it is not irritated, joking, fearful (the trial is over and won) or a statement of thanks.

exclusions.A: The chimney I know is only the stump of the one Reyburn knew, and the evenings when ten thousand swifts poured into it are gone for good.
exclusions.D: The shortened flue holds a few hundred birds at most.
exclusions.E: In early October the birds will leave for the south, and in May they will return to the same stump.

support: The chimney I know is only the stump of the one Reyburn knew, and the evenings when ten thousand swifts poured into it are gone for good.
Each September evening the few hundred that remain drop into it within a few minutes, and then the sky over Linden Row is empty long before the old flocks would have finished coming down.
WV12-P04.5.note: The writer dwells on the lost full chimney and its vanished ten-thousand-bird evenings ('gone for good', 'the sky over Linden Row is empty'), a literal statement of loss with no ironic or teasing reading; 'The stump is sound' approves the repair of the stump, not admiration of the old chimney, so A is not separately defensible.
